sections.html:
Lancaster County hugs the North Carolina border in the Piedmont and is part of the Charlotte metro area. The City of Lancaster is the seat. Up in the northern panhandle, Indian Land is a big unincorporated community of 32,759 people (2020). Countywide, the 2020 census found 96,016 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 114,296.

A new house in the growing north and an older house on acreage elsewhere in the county attract different buyers, yet both are taxed and recorded through the same handful of county offices.

Current taxes are the County Treasurer's job, handled at the County Administration Building, 101 North Main Street, Lancaster. When real property is still unpaid after the March deadline, the Tax Collector's Office takes it over.

Office or serviceContact

Payment is accepted in cash, by check, or by card at the counter, plus online (lancastersctax.qpaybill.com), by phone and by mail. A 2.35 percent convenience fee on cards goes to the service provider, and a returned payment is charged $30. More detail is at lancastercountysc.gov.

No penalty applies to real estate or personal property tax paid by January 15. Should the 15th be a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, you have until 5 pm on the following business day. Bills reach mailboxes at least 30 days ahead.

March 16 is the handoff date to the Tax Collector's Office for anything still owed, adjusted when it lands on a weekend or holiday. Vehicle bills run separately and come due at month end, mailed a month in advance.

State law sets the penalty rates: one charge once the due date passes, with more added in February and again in March. See Section 12-45-180. It also makes the postmark the test for a mailed payment. Phone the Treasurer for the dollar amounts on your own bill.

  • After a mid-year transfer, a new owner who got no timely notice has protection, since the statute forces the treasurer to waive penalties.
  • A wrong postmark can be excused when you have proof.

Everything starts with a letter to the County Assessor, mailed within 90 days of the notice date. State law sets the stages that follow.

  1. Ask the Assessor for a conference, which should be scheduled within a month.
  2. After the conference, you have 30 days to file a written protest.
  3. The Assessor answers in writing, normally within 30 days.
  4. Take the dispute to the county board no later than 30 days after that answer.
  5. Within 30 days of the board's decision you can ask the Administrative Law Court for a contested case hearing.

A case that is unfinished on December 31 is billed at 80 percent of the protested value until it ends. Sections 12-60-2510 to 12-60-2550 hold the full text. A separate rule, Section 12-43-217, puts counties on a five-year reappraisal cycle and requires notice to owners when value or class moves by $1,000 or more.

Where the owner lives in the house, 4 percent of fair market value is the taxable amount, and up to five contiguous acres come along with it. The application must reach the county by the first penalty date of your first claim year. More than 72 rental days in a year ends eligibility.

After you sell, the buyer applies on their own. An improper claim costs 100 percent of the tax paid, plus interest. Farm land can get 4 percent too, but a switch in use brings rollback taxes for this year and the three before. Chapter 43 of Title 12 has the details.

Indian Land has no downtown and lies about six miles east of Fort Mill. U.S. 521 and SC 160 are its main roads, and no public transportation serves it. A 2014 overlay district sets design rules for new construction along those corridors.

Because Indian Land is not a town, county offices serve every house there. A seller with acreage should ask the Assessor whether agricultural classification applies before listing, since that status affects rollback taxes.

sections.h2: Other offices and the deed fee
sections.html:
Call the county's main number, 803-285-1565, if you are unsure where to start. Most sellers deal with these offices at the County Administration Building, 101 North Main Street:

  • Treasurer: current taxes and payment.
  • Tax Collector: past-due real property after the March deadline.
  • Assessor: value, classification and appeals.
  • Development Services: permits and land use.

Permit and zoning questions are answered by the county's Code of Ordinances, which is posted on the county site. The deed fee is $1.85 per $500 of value: $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county, normally the seller's cost. Foreclosure and deed in lieu transfers to a mortgage holder are exempt, per Title 12, Chapter 24.

Overdue taxes slow a sale without stopping it. A workable sequence:

  1. Before March 16, call the Treasurer at 803-285-7939. After it, call the Tax Collector at 803-283-8885.
  2. Request a payoff valid through the date you expect to close, because the amount moves on penalty dates.
  3. Ask the Assessor whether the parcel has the 4 percent rate or an agricultural classification.
  4. Hand the figure to the title company, which settles with the county out of your proceeds.

Paying cash and buying as-is lets a buyer skip the lender appraisal, so timing depends mostly on title work and the payoff. An inherited house needs its estate paperwork in order, which closing agents normally request up front.

Plan on a few phone calls rather than a trip downtown. Almost every question on this page can be answered by one of the numbers listed above, and the Treasurer accepts payment by phone.

sections.h2: What to have ready for closing
sections.html:
Preparation saves time. Round up the deed or tax map number, the newest tax bill and a photo ID before contacting an office. If the account is behind, write down the payoff figure along with the date it was quoted. Penalties step up on fixed dates, so a figure from January will not match one from March.

Confirm that your legal residence application is on file, and let the buyer know they must file their own. If the property includes acreage with a farm classification, find out from the Assessor what rollback tax would be due if the use changes after the sale. Keep a copy of the closing statement showing the county was paid.

faqs.q: What is the due date for Lancaster County property tax?
faqs.a: Payment is penalty-free through January 15 for real estate and personal property alike. A weekend or holiday on that date moves the cutoff to the next business day. Notices go out 30 days or more beforehand.

faqs.q: Where do I pay my Lancaster County tax bill?
faqs.a: At 101 N Main Street in Lancaster, on the web at lancastersctax.qpaybill.com, by phone at 803-797-2853, or by mail to P.O. Box 729, Lancaster, SC 29720.

faqs.q: Where do unpaid taxes go after March 16?
faqs.a: To the Tax Collector's Office, 803-283-8885. Get a payoff figure there before closing.

faqs.q: Does paying by card cost extra in Lancaster County?
faqs.a: Yes. A 2.35 percent convenience fee applies and goes to the service provider rather than the county. A returned payment is $30.

faqs.q: What is the first step to dispute my Lancaster County value?
faqs.a: Mail the County Assessor a written objection no later than 90 days after the notice date, then follow the protest and board stages. The Assessor's office can supply forms.
